answer.rationale: With the line at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, switching primary vendor now (memory_c2's cost win) carries onboarding/integration risk that could breach delivery commitments during a 14-day contract cliff. Memory_c1 and c6 show the incumbent relationship has historically preserved integration stability and can yield volume-based cost reductions, while memory_c4 shows that benchmarking-driven renegotiation at a prior renewal already recovered real margin and improved terms without changing suppliers. Given the mandate is 18% and the low-cost quote meets it only in isolation (ignoring switching/integration risk to TCO), the lower-risk path to the mandate is to renegotiate hard with the incumbent using competitive benchmarks (including the low-cost quote) as leverage, preserving delivery continuity while pushing for the required savings. I verified c4 (precedent for successful benchmarked renegotiation) and c2 (to check how clean the vendor-switch precedent really was, since it's the main tempting alternative) before committing. Switching or adding a second source is deferred to next cycle pending more capacity to manage transition risk safely.
